label: Spanish and American troops near the Sabine, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The special session of 1797: Adams's summoning proclamation (25 March), his speech (16 May) and the House's answer. Contains the speech, proclamation and answer groups.
label: Special session of Congress, 1797

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The President's proclamation of 30 July 1807 calling Congress to meet on 26 October instead of in December, and his message to the session on 27 October. Contains those two groups.
label: Congress called early, 1807

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the House of Representatives' answer to Adams's speech of 16 May 1797, in draft and final form.
label: House's answer to the special-session speech

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of Adams's proclamation of 25 March 1797 convening Congress on 15 May.
label: Proclamation summoning Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of the Lords Commissioners to both Houses of Parliament on 21 January 1806, made in the King's name: 'In pursuance of the authority given to us by his Majesty's Commission under the Great Seal, among other things, to declare the cause of his holding this Parliament'. It speaks of the success of the King's arms at sea and of the war on the Continent. The British government's statement. Two papers printed only a part of it, headed 'His Majesty's Message'.
label: The speech opening Parliament, 21 January 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 10 May 1806: 'We learn from a gentleman who arrived in this city a day or two ago, from St. Domingo, that at the time of his departure there were very general movements among the subjects of the black emperor Dessalines'; the cause was not known, 'but it was said that some advices had been received by way of Jamaica'. A traveller's report at second hand, in the paper's words.
label: A Philadelphia report of movements in St. Domingo, May 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Reports of the meeting of a committee of Congress (Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge) with Lord Howe on Staten Island in September 1776: their setting off, and the committee's report to Congress. Contains those two groups.
label: Staten Island peace conference

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of Caleb Strong, Governor of Massachusetts, to the two houses of the legislature, June 1805: 'I embrace with pleasure the opportunity of congratulating you on the return of the anniversary, established by our Constitution'. He speaks of debtors, land disputes in the eastern counties, banks, and Kentucky's proposed amendment on the federal courts. A governor's own policy argument.
label: Governor Strong's speech to the Massachusetts legislature

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of a letter to the settlers on the Watauga and Nolachucky rivers, signed 'Henry Stuart, Deputy Superintendent', for the British superintendent of Indian affairs in the southern district, with a sworn statement that a stranger delivered it on 18 May 1776. The letter invites those 'willing to join his Majesty's forces, as soon as they arrive at the Cherokee nation' to sign a paper of allegiance, and says that the King will land an army in West Florida and march it through the Creek nation to the Chickasaws, 'where 500 warriors from each nation are to join them', and on by the Cherokees, 'who have also promised their assistance'. The papers printed it in June and July as a letter delivered to the frontier inhabitants, and from late August among papers sent from Augusta, Georgia, as 'an intercepted letter'. One side's letter, as printed.
label: Henry Stuart's letter to the frontier inhabitants, May 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London Sun of 10 April 1793: it was rumoured that Dumouriez, having found reason to doubt his army's promises to support his plan of marching to Paris and placing young Louis on the throne, had left it at the head of a regiment of cavalry. A rumour, labelled as one. Several papers print it with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received'), the others among London paragraphs.
label: The Sun of 10 April: Dumouriez rumoured to have left his army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a 'Swedish bulletin' from the headquarters of the Swedish army, April 1806, from London papers: reports 'received from adjutant general count Lowenhielm' said the Prussians had taken several villages near Lauenburg, and on the 23rd 'the Prussians passed the Lauenburg frontier'. One army's own account.
label: A Swedish bulletin: the Prussians cross into Lauenburg

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a New York report (end of July 1776) that about fifteen inhabitants drove off five boats from the men of war trying to land on Tappan meadows.
label: Boats driven off at Tappan

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the report of Littleton W. Tazewell to the Mayor of Norfolk (5 July 1807) on delivering the Mayor's answer on board the Bellona: Douglas said his letter had been misapprehended and that he intended no menace. Includes one shorter account of the report.
label: Tazewell's report to the Mayor

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings of this report, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a Norfolk report, from a passenger on the Danish ship Christian Haven, that the British attack on Santa Cruz de Tenerife (July 1797) was driven off. Other Tenerife accounts in the collection are different texts and are not included.
label: Tenerife defeat report

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the thirtieth bulletin of the French Grand Army, dated Austerlitz, 12 Frimaire, year 14 (3 December 1805): 'The 6th Frimaire, the emperor, upon receiving the communication of the full powers of Messrs. de Stadion and de Giulay, offered previously an armistice'. The French army's official account of the battle.
label: The thirtieth bulletin of the Grand Army

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a bulletin from the London Gazette, dated Tournai, 3 May 1793: on the 1st the French attacked the advanced posts of the left wing and of the centre of the combined army and were repulsed, with the loss of men and cannon. The British government's own account. Four papers print it after another Tournai paragraph on the preparations against Condé.
label: The London Gazette from Tournai, 3 May: the French attacks repulsed

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The President's message to the Senate of 10 January 1806 with the French government's complaints against American trade with St. Domingo, and the act of 28 February 1806 that prohibited trade with the parts of the island 'not in possession, and under the acknowledged government of France'. Contains those two groups.
label: Trade with St. Domingo: the French complaints and the act of 28 February 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Treasury Department's circular to the collectors of the customs, dated 3 March 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'I herewith transmit a printed copy of an act to interdict the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France', with directions section by section on how the collectors are to carry it out.
label: The Treasury's circular of 3 March 1809 on the non-intercourse act

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Treasury's circular to the collectors of the customs, 9 August 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'You will herewith receive the copy of a Proclamation of the President'; the act of 28 June now applies to Great Britain as to France, 'any thing in my circular of 29th June last, to the contrary, notwithstanding', with rules for vessels that sailed on the faith of the April proclamation.
label: The Treasury's circular to the collectors, 9 August 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round two, 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of the circular of the Secretary of the Treasury to the collectors of the customs (Philadelphia, 4 August 1793): as repeated contraventions of neutrality had taken place in American ports, the collectors were to watch for vessels arming or equipping for the powers at war, with the schedule of 'Rules adopted by the President' on arming, equipping and prizes. The circular and its rules are one publication. An official document.
label: Hamilton's circular to the collectors, with the President's rules on neutrality

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Secretary of the Treasury's report to Congress, sent 7 December 1809: Albert Gallatin's letter of transmittal and the report 'prepared in obedience to the act … to establish the Treasury Department', on the revenue of 1807 to 1809 and the expenses, with the statement that 'a loan will be necessary' unless the military and naval expenses are reduced.
label: The Secretary of the Treasury's annual report, December 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the treaty of peace between Austria and France signed at Pressburg on 26 December 1805: 'His majesty the emperor of Germany and Austria, and his majesty the emperor of the French, king of Italy, equally animated with a desire to put an end to the calamities of war'. Some papers printed it with the Emperor Napoleon's act of ratification before it. A treaty.
label: The treaty of Pressburg between Austria and France

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the treaty of peace between France and Austria signed at Vienna on 14 October 1809, with Napoleon's ratification before it ('Having seen and considered the treaty concluded, determined and signed at Vienna, on the 14th of this month'): the lands Austria gives up, a 'full and complete pardon for the inhabitants of the Tyrol', and the times for the French troops to leave.
label: The treaty of peace between France and Austria, Vienna, 14 October 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two letters on the American squadron's attacks on Tripoli in August and September 1804, as the 1805 papers printed them after the President sent them to Congress: Richard O'Brien's letter from Malta of 5 September 1804 (sent on 31 December 1804) and Commodore Preble's letter of 18 September 1804 (sent on 20 February 1805). Contains those two groups. Each is an American official's own account.
label: Letters on the squadron before Tripoli, sent to Congress

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter to the French Executive Directory dated 6 November 1796 and signed Truguet: 'I hasten to communicate to the Executive Directory the reception of letters from Brest, of the 3d instant (November) brought by an extraordinary courier, which announce that a general revolution has just taken place in Ireland.' It gives the report of the captains of two ships brought in from Liverpool by French privateers, that the Irish had taken 30,000 stand of arms in Dublin and defeated 10,000 English troops. Printed from the Paris papers, in the same column of French news as General Bournonville's letter (a group of its own). A report at second hand: the writer passes on what letters from Brest and two ship captains said.
label: Truguet to the Directory, 6 November 1796: letters from Brest 'announce that a general revolution has just taken place in Ireland'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress on the dispute with Tunis, read in the House on 14 April 1806: 'During the blockade of Tripoli by the squadron of the U. S. a small cruiser, under the flag of Tunis, with two prizes' tried to enter the port. The executive's own account.
label: The President's message on Tunis, April 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 passages describing the Two Sisters wreck off Bantry Bay, checked against the scan.
definition: Printed accounts of the Rhode Island ship Two Sisters found wrecked off Bantry Bay in August 1797: a reprinted hand-bill and a summary attributed to the Irish papers. Different wording; the wreck itself is not independently verified.
label: Two Sisters wreck

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter to the editor of the Moniteur (the Louisiana Monitor) of New Orleans, dated 12 September 1804: 'The following memorial was addressed by the Ursuline Nuns of this city to the President of the United States', with the memorial ('Emboldened by the favourable mention you have been pleased to make of their Order, the Nuns of Ursula ...') and the President's answer ('I have received, holy Sisters, the letter you have written me, wherein you express anxiety for the property vested in your institution, by the former governments of Louisiana'). Jenks' Portland Gazette prints the memorial and the answer without the letter to the editor. The nuns' and the President's own words.
label: The Ursuline nuns of New Orleans to the President, and his answer, 1804

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph dated Strasburgh, 17 November 1805, from French papers that reached New York in January 1806: 'The city of Vienna has just opened its gates for the first time to a victorious army. This glory was reserved for Frenchmen.' A report from the French side.
label: Strasburgh, 17 November 1805: Vienna opens its gates

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Vienna dated 26 July 1797, printed from the London papers in two forms. Three papers print a short form: 'The Marquis DE GALLO, has this moment arrived here from Udina. The negotiations for peace in Italy, meet with great difficulties. The French require that Mantua shall be united with the Cisalpine Republic' (the Mirror's words). The Gazette of the United States and the Kentucky Gazette print a longer form that opens with the Marquis de Gallo's conferences with the Emperor and Baron Thugut, and adds that 'neither the marquis nor the persons about the court had very pleasant countenances'. Both forms then give the same account of the French demand for Mantua, the Emperor's indemnification in Istria and Dalmatia, and 'our fears that hostilities may again commence'. A correspondent's report, at second hand through the London papers.
label: Vienna, 26 July 1797: the peace talks in Italy 'meet with great difficulties'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the Virginia Convention's resolutions of 15 May 1776, which instructed the colony's delegates to propose that Congress declare the colonies free and independent states.
label: Virginia Convention, 15 May 1776

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a publication from the Philadelphia Political Register, dated 20 September 1804 in two papers: 'In the discharge of an important, and to myself an indispensable duty, the subjoined statement was communicated, in the first instance, to the government.—In a respectful solicitude for the rights and interest of our country the deposition and letters are now made public. W. Jackson.' The statement, deposition and letters that follow concern the Marquis de Casa Yrujo, the Spanish minister. One side's own account.
label: W. Jackson's statement in the Political Register, September 1804, with a deposition and letters concerning the Spanish minister

admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the War Department's circular to the state governors, 29 April 1809: 'I am directed by the President of the United States to inform your Excellency that the detachment of ... Militia, made in pursuance of a communication to your Excellency from this Department' may be discharged. The papers print the copies sent to different governors (10,198 men for Virginia). The Portland Gazette calls it a circular 'for disbanding the Militia'.
label: The War Department's circular to the governors on the militia, 29 April 1809

admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the 6-paper threshold for 1793).
definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of early September 1793: by an express to the War Office from the commissioners for treating with the Indian nations north of the Ohio, they 'were not able even to effect a meeting' with the nations assembled at the rapids of the Miami river; the nations' deputation 'insisted upon the Ohio as the boundary between them and the United States', and, 'as so extensive a concession was inadmissible', the commissioners left on 17 August. It names the Wyandots, Delawares, Shawanese and Miamis as 'determined for war', says that a considerable part of them were for peace, and that the Six Nations, with Captain Brandt (Brant) and his Mohawks, urged peace. The United States government's account, as the papers printed it.
label: The War Office on the treaty commissioners, September 1793

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the account of the interview of 20 July 1776 between General Washington and Colonel Patterson, General Howe's adjutant general.
label: Washington meets Colonel Patterson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Two reports from Natchez, in the Mississippi Territory, of an armed party that marched from near the line with Spanish West Florida against the fort of Baton Rouge in August 1804 and posted a paper declaring West Florida free. Contains those two groups.
label: An armed party marches against the Spanish fort of Baton Rouge in West Florida, August 1804: two reports from Natchez

admission_rule: Reviewed 1800 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a paragraph of London news: 'It was on the 29th ult. that Lord Whitworth signed the Convention with Count Bernstorff, the Danish Minister. The following is a note written by his Lordship to one of our Ministers abroad on the subject', followed by the note ('I have the satisfaction to acquaint you that I yesterday signed a convention with the Danish Minister, on terms satisfactory to his Majesty') and, in most papers, what the London paper gives as its principal articles: 'The Danish frigate and convoy, carried into Deal, shall be repaired at the expense of Great-Britain, and then released', and the question of the right to visit convoys adjourned to a negotiation in London. A London paper's report with the British envoy's own note.
label: London, September 1800: Lord Whitworth's convention with Denmark, and his note

admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the speech of John Wilkes, Lord Mayor of London, in the House of Commons on the motion for an address to the King at the opening of the session in October 1775, against the war in America.
label: Wilkes's speech in the Commons

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Documents and reports of the charges that General James Wilkinson had taken money from the Spanish government, as the 1808 papers printed them: his challenge to John Randolph and Randolph's answer (December 1807), Daniel Clark's statement to the House, the President's message of 20 January, and the opinion of the military court of inquiry (printed from 4 July). Contains those four groups. The statement and the letters are allegations and each writer's own account; the court found no evidence.
label: Charges against General Wilkinson, 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the opinion of the military court of inquiry at Washington on General Wilkinson (signed by its president, Colonel Burbeck, and approved by the President), printed from 4 July 1808: it found no evidence that Wilkinson had received a pension or money from the Spanish government for corrupt purposes.
label: The court of inquiry's opinion on Wilkinson

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of notes exchanged at Baltimore on 26 and 27 October 1808, as published there: General James Wilkinson's note to Captain Robert Goodloe Harper, commanding a company of volunteer artillery, charging that Harper had 'secretly assailed the General's honour' and demanding 'the only admissible atonement'; Harper's refusal, which says that his advice to Mr. Clark to lay before Congress documents on Wilkinson's 'connection with the Spanish government' gave no ground for a challenge; and Wilkinson's reply. Each man's own words. The papers print them under their own introductions or headings, such as 'MODERN CHIVALRY' and '"HECTOR" AGAIN.'
label: General Wilkinson's challenge to Robert Goodloe Harper, October 1808

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter of General Wilkinson, dated Rapids of Red River, 19 September 1806: 'My orders, and the conduct of the Mexicans, are so much at variance'; 'I fear you will be informed blood has been spilt'. The American commander's own account, with his forecast.
label: General Wilkinson's letter from the Rapids of Red River, 19 September

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract from the orders of General Wilkinson 'given at the camp of the American troops, on the left bank of the Mississippi, near the city of New Orleans, Dec. 17, 1803', with the parole 'Columbia': 'The operation before us, however simple or safe, will require much self denial and restraint'; the orders tell the troops how they are to conduct themselves on entering the city. A commander's orders, as printed.
label: General Wilkinson's orders at the camp near New Orleans, 17 December 1803: 'The operation before us, however simple or safe, will require much self denial and restraint'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1808 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of two letters of 24 and 25 December 1807, from a pamphlet: General James Wilkinson asks John Randolph, a member of the House, for satisfaction for words injurious to his reputation, and Randolph refuses. Each letter is its writer's own account.
label: Wilkinson's challenge and Randolph's answer

admission_rule: Reviewed 1807 printings, checked against the scan (round two: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).
definition: Printings of General Wilkinson's address to the court at New Orleans, as a letter from that city of 18 December 1806 reports it (Washington, 21 January 1807): appearing on a writ of habeas corpus for a man he had arrested, he said he was 'called to account for an act in which I glory', warned that 'the artifices of the confederates' must no longer 'cheat the public judgment' and that 'treason stalks abroad', and spoke of 'the friends of Burr and rebellion'. The report adds that he then charged two lawyers with being parties to the conspiracy. The general's own words, as the letter gives them.
label: General Wilkinson's speech in the court at New Orleans

admission_rule: Reviewed 1797 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a report from Wilmington, North Carolina, of 12 October 1797: 'A gentleman who arrived in town on Sunday last from New-Providence, via the Havannah, has favored the Printer with the following information—on the authenticity of which he places the greatest confidence': on 20 August, the day he left Pensacola, he saw an official letter from the Baron de Carondelet saying that orders had come from his court 'to put into full execution, the treaty between Spain and the United States of America', and that the commandants of the forts on the Mississippi were to deliver up the posts; Governor Gayoso had been appointed governor-general of the Floridas and Louisiana. A traveller's report at second hand.
label: Wilmington, 12 October 1797: a traveller from Pensacola reports orders to deliver up the Spanish posts

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Wythe Court-House, Virginia, to his friend in Frederick-Town, Maryland, dated 30 July 1804: 'We have for 12 days been clouded with a dark smoke, and this day I was informed by a gentleman from Kentucky that the Clinch Mountain had sunk for many miles to the depth of 50 feet'; the writer supposes it 'occasioned by the burning of the stone coal which is in the mountain'. Two papers print a shorter form headed 'Singular Phenomenon', without the date and with 'for ten days'; the Rhode-Island Republican also prints 'ten days', and the Norfolk Gazette 'twelve days' in words. A report at second hand: the writer passes on what a traveller told him.
label: A letter from Wythe Court-House, Virginia, 30 July 1804: 'the Clinch Mountain had sunk'

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo, Spain's minister to the United States, and the American government in January 1806: his circular to the other foreign ministers against the President's message, and the letter in which the Secretary of State told him that the President expected his departure, with his answers. Contains those two groups.
label: The Spanish minister Yrujo and the government, 1806

admission_rule: Reviewed 1806 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of the circular of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo to the foreign ministers in the United States, dated Philadelphia, 21 January 1806, in a translation from the French: 'The want of correctness which appears to prevail throughout the article, relative to Spain, of the message' of the President. With his note to the Secretary of State. The Spanish minister's own account.
label: Yrujo's circular to the foreign ministers

admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.
definition: Printings of a letter from the Spanish minister to the Secretary of State, published in the National Intelligencer of 5 October 1804 'at the request of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo': 'Having been absent from Philadelphia for these 18 days past and travelled far into a part of Virginia where I had no opportunity to see the late newspapers from the Northward', he answers the publication in the Political Register (the other group). The minister's own account; the New Hampshire Gazette and the Kentucky Gazette misprint his name 'Trujo' (their transcriptions read 'Trujillo'), and the Oracle Post prints the letter over two issues.
label: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo's letter to the Secretary of State, published at his request, October 1804
